strings.L-7: Answer from what you already know. Don’t open the boiler to check. For immediate danger, get outside and call 911.
strings.L-8: The other check already covered gas, CO, and smoke. These are boiler-only. Answer from what you already know.
strings.L-9: Answer for the people at home right now. Pick the first one that fits.
strings.L-10: With someone fragile at home in cold weather, no heat needs a pro now.
strings.L-11:
Look at the round gauge on the boiler or a nearby pipe. Many show psi and temperature together. Some combis show bar: 1 bar is about 14.5 psi.

Many makers ask for about 12 psi or more when the system is cold, and not over about 24 to 25 psi when hot. Your manual’s numbers come first. Don’t tap or adjust anything.
strings.L-12: Look at the glass tube on the side of the boiler from a step back. Don’t touch it or its valves; it can be hot. The water level moves a little while the boiler runs.
strings.L-13: An empty or unreadable steam-boiler sight glass may mean dangerously low water. Stop using the boiler and call for urgent service. Do not add water, even after it cools.
strings.L-14:
Write down the exact code and the boiler’s brand and model, or take a photo. Your owner’s manual explains it.

Pick the closest match. Don’t reset anything on this screen.
strings.L-15: A reset is only for a lockout your owner’s manual tells you to reset, from the front of the boiler. Pick the first one that fits.
strings.L-16:
- **These steps are optional.** You can stop and call a licensed HVAC professional at any time.
- **Write down or photograph how things are set now.** You’ll need it to put things back.
- **Do only the step shown, the way it’s shown.** Don’t open panels, use tools on the equipment, or change anything else, even if it’s on the same screen or nearby.
- **If anything looks different from these steps, stop.** Your equipment may not match what we describe. Check your owner’s manual.
- **If you smell gas or burning, hear a CO alarm, see smoke, or see water near wires, stop now** and use the emergency steps.
- These steps come from the equipment maker’s documents and common trade practice. They’re general information, not a diagnosis or an inspection of your system.
strings.L-17:
**Reset once, only once.** If it stops or shows the same code again, don’t reset it again. Repeated shutdowns mean a safety device is doing its job. Call a licensed HVAC professional and tell them the code and what you saw.

We show resets only for owner’s manuals we’ve checked. If yours isn’t listed, skip the reset.
strings.L-17a:
1. On the screen, select **MANUAL RESET**.
2. On the next screen, press **Reset**.
strings.L-17b:
1. If the reset button is flashing, press and hold it until the display changes, as your manual shows.
2. If it isn’t flashing, switch the boiler **OFF** and **ON** again, the way your manual shows.
strings.L-17c:
1. Press and hold the **Reset** button for about 5 seconds.
2. The display shows **rE** while it resets.
strings.L-17d: 1. Press the blinking button once: **Central Heating** or **Domestic Hot Water**.
strings.L-17e:
1. On the home screen, tap **Unlock**.
2. Tap **OK** twice to confirm.
strings.L-19: If you can’t rule out a hazard, stop the check.
strings.L-20:
1. With the cold zone’s thermostat calling for heat, find that zone’s valve on the pipes near the boiler. Many are labeled by zone.
2. Look at the light on top. Don’t press the button on top or move any lever.
strings.L-21: Your installer may want to make this change to keep coverage in place.
strings.L-22:
1. Write down the boiler gauge reading. Set the thermostat to Off, and wait until the radiators are cool to the touch.
2. Find the small vent at the top or end of the cold radiator or baseboard. Some baseboard vents sit behind a hinged end cap. Use only the radiator key made for the vent, or a coin for a coin-slot vent.
3. Hold a cup and a towel under it. Turn the vent slowly until air hisses out.
4. When water flows steadily for a few seconds, close the vent.
5. Read the gauge again. Then set the thermostat back the way you wrote it down.
strings.L-23: A vent that won’t close keeps letting water out, and the pressure will drop.
strings.L-24: Thermostats use different battery-access arrangements, and some do not use batteries. The model-specific thermostat check can help identify yours. Do not pull an unfamiliar faceplate or expose wires.
strings.L-25: Never heat with an oven, stove, grill, or generator indoors (carbon monoxide). If you use an electric space heater, plug it straight into a wall outlet, follow its maker’s instructions, and keep it clear of anything that can burn.
strings.L-26: The pressure check needs a reading you can see without opening anything.
strings.L-27: An indirect tank receives heat from the boiler. Neither side has been confirmed to work. Use only what you have already noticed during normal hot-water use. Do not run a hot tap as a test, touch hot pipes, or change the tank’s temperature dial.
strings.L-28: Look, don’t touch. From where you already stand, look toward the pipe that carries hot water into the air handler. Answer from what you have already noticed in ordinary use. Do not hold a hand near the pipe, grab it, or touch it. Do not open a cover or move insulation.
strings.L-29: The checks differ for hot-water and steam boilers.
strings.L-30: It may have been turned off on purpose, so ask a pro before it goes back on.
strings.L-31: A blocked vent can stop the boiler or push exhaust and carbon monoxide back inside.
strings.L-33:
You’ve done the homeowner checks this guide offers. What’s left is inside the boiler or its piping, and that’s work for a licensed heating pro.

Don’t press reset buttons, keep restarting the boiler, add water, or open any boiler door or panel. If it’s acting strangely, set the thermostat to Off.

The next screen has a note to share with the pro.
strings.L-34:
Use what you already know, a manual, or a label you can read without opening anything.

Plastic (white or gray) vent pipes out a wall usually mean a high-efficiency boiler. A metal pipe into a chimney usually means a standard boiler.
strings.L-35: The homeowner checks are done. The next checks are inside the boiler or its piping.
strings.L-40: Use only what you have already noticed in ordinary use. Do not run hot water as a test, touch pipes, or change boiler settings. A combi boiler serves two demands; working room heat does not prove hot-water operation.
strings.L-41: The home has enough heat; the tap hot water is the problem
strings.L-42: Don’t press reset buttons, restart, add water, or open panels.
strings.L-43: Do not add water, even after it cools.
strings.L-44: Water near wiring can shock, and a boiler that has been under water needs its controls checked before it runs.
strings.L-45: A refrigerant leak alarm needs people out of the affected area. This boiler check does not identify the refrigerant or the cause.
strings.L-46: A gas or rotten-egg smell in the air, a gasoline, paint, or solvent smell near the boiler, or a strong smell I can’t place
strings.L-46-fact: Gas, rotten-egg in air, flammable-vapor, or unknown strong smell reported.
strings.L-46e: A rotten-egg or sulfur smell that may be only from the hot water
strings.L-46h: One quick question about where you smell it. If it’s in the air, choose the gas choice above.
strings.L-46f: Rotten-egg or sulfur smell reported; asked where.
strings.L-47: Where do you notice the rotten-egg or sulfur smell?
strings.L-47b: Answer from what you already know. Don’t go near the boiler or its gas line to check. If you have any doubt, choose Not sure.
strings.L-47a: I hear hissing, there’s a problem with the pilot, or someone has a headache
strings.L-47a-f: Egg/sulfur smell with hissing, a pilot problem, or a headache reported.
strings.L-47air: I smell it in the air near the boiler or gas lines, or anywhere in the house, even with no water running.
strings.L-47air-f: Egg/sulfur smell in the air reported.
strings.L-47n-f: Not sure where the egg/sulfur smell is.
strings.L-47t: Only when hot water runs from a faucet; cold water and the air smell fine.
strings.L-47t-h: The water heater check takes it from here.
strings.L-47t-f: Egg/sulfur smell only from hot water reported (homeowner report).
strings.L-7f: (Most home hot-water boilers have a 30 psi relief valve, and steam boilers 15 psi.)
strings.L-7f-source: MANUAL: Weil-McLain Evergreen Series 2 User’s Information Manual 550-100-580/0325, page 6 (hot water): “Make sure the pressure reading on the boiler pressure/temperature gauge does not exceed 24 psig if using a 30 psig relief valve (typical installation).” Weil-McLain SGO Series 4 Boiler Manual 550-142-330/0225, page 7 (steam): “Incorrect or defective relief valve. Check for proper relief valve (15 psi).” Checked October 20, 2026.
strings.D-056a: Don’t touch light switches or phones, or use lighters, matches, or anything that could spark or flame while you’re inside.
strings.L-34-where: Look at the pipe where it leaves the boiler. Don’t touch it or put your hand on or near it. If the boiler is running but that zone’s rooms stay cold, note what you see and call a licensed HVAC professional.
